841.title: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
841.hook: in the duel with Arjuna, the earth takes hold of Karna's wheel
841.tomorrow: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
841.howItsDone: The scene of Karna on foot, straining to lift his sunken chariot wheel, is retold in recitations, plays and serials of the Mahabharata, along with the curses behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Arjuna nearly drew his sword on his own brother, and Krishna asked what truth is for. Your line was the brothers weep, and Yudhishthira blesses him.

Karna and Arjuna, at last, face to face. Karna fits a terrible arrow to his bow, an arrow with a serpent in it, the epic says, a snake with an old grudge against Arjuna. Shalya, at the reins, gives him advice: aim for the chest. Karna refuses. He doesn't aim twice, he says, and he looses at Arjuna's head. And Krishna, driving the other chariot, presses down with his feet, and the chariot sinks into the earth, just enough. The serpent arrow takes Arjuna's crown and leaves Arjuna alive. Hold on to that sinking chariot.
screen: `THE SERPENT ARROW.` → `AIM FOR THE CHEST.` → `KRISHNA PRESSES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The duel goes on, and then the earth takes hold of Karna's chariot wheel. It sinks, and it stays sunk. The chariot lurches and won't move. In the same moment, Karna reaches in memory for his great weapon, and it isn't there. He can't remember the words. The epic explains both with old curses. Long before, Karna had killed a Brahmin's cow by accident, and the Brahmin cursed him: at the moment you most need it, the earth will swallow your wheel. And Karna had once trained under the great teacher Parashurama, hiding that he wasn't a Brahmin. When the teacher found out, he cursed him to forget the weapon he'd learned in the hour he most needed it. Two old debts, the epic says, come due on the same afternoon. Notice the echo. When Krishna pressed his chariot into the earth, the sinking saved Arjuna's life. Now the earth holds Karna's wheel, and the sinking will cost him his. Karna jumps down from the chariot. He grips the wheel with both hands and tries to lift it out of the ground: the commander of the Kaurava army, on foot, straining at a wheel.
screen: `THE EARTH HOLDS THE WHEEL` · `THE WEAPON FORGOTTEN` · `TWO OLD CURSES COME DUE` · then, large: `KARNA LIFTS THE WHEEL`

segments.voice: Put both feet flat on the floor and press down gently; feel the ground press back. Let something that feels stuck come to mind, and don't try to lift it yet, just notice where it sits and how heavy it is. If you pray, you can bring what's stuck into your prayer.
Karna. The warrior whose wheel sinks and whose weapon slips from memory, at the moment he needs them most.

842.title: Karna: the wheel stuck, the death
842.hook: Karna appeals to the rules of war, and Krishna answers with questions
842.carry: he hangs his head in shame, and says nothing
842.tomorrow: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
842.howItsDone: Karna's death is retold in readings, regional theater, poems and serials, and Karna is discussed as a figure hard to judge: generous, loyal, wronged at birth, and complicit in wrong.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna's wheel sank into the earth and his weapon slipped from memory. Your line was two old curses at once.

Wait. That's what Karna calls out, standing on the ground with his hands on the wheel. Wait, Arjuna. A warrior in a chariot shouldn't strike a man who is on foot, whose wheel is stuck, who isn't ready. Those are the rules of fair fighting, he says, in effect. Remember dharma. Give me a moment to free the wheel. By the rules the armies agreed to, it sounds like a fair request, made by a man in real trouble. And it isn't Arjuna who answers. It's Krishna, from the driver's seat.

Krishna's answer is a string of questions. Now you remember dharma, Karna? Where was it when Draupadi was dragged into the assembly hall and you mocked her? Where was it at the rigged game of dice? Where was it when young Abhimanyu was surrounded by many warriors at once and cut down? In Ganguli's English, Karna hears this, and he hangs his head in shame, and says nothing. He doesn't argue. He climbs back into the stuck chariot and fights on as well as he can. Then Arjuna, urged on by Krishna, takes up a single great arrow and cuts off Karna's head. Karna falls. And the epic gives one more picture: a light rises from his body and goes up into the sky, into the sun. Karna was, as the epic told it long before, a son of the sun god. Hold both halves of this man together, because the story does. The Karna who kept his promise to Kunti, and the Karna who laughed at Draupadi. The friend who never left Duryodhana, and the man who stood by while wrong was done. One more thing. The Pandavas, cheering on the field, still don't know who just died. Kunti knows. Her sons will learn after the war that they have killed their eldest brother.
screen: `NOW YOU REMEMBER DHARMA?` · `KARNA HANGS HIS HEAD` · `THE LIGHT GOES TO THE SUN` · then, large: `A BROTHER THEY DIDN'T KNOW`

843.title: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
843.hook: after Karna, an old teacher pleads for peace, and Duryodhana says no
843.tomorrow: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
843.howItsDone: The Shalya Parva, the epic's book named for Shalya, is read and recited with the rest of the Mahabharata; Kripa's plea for peace and Duryodhana's refusal are retold as a turning point before the war's last day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Karna died beside his stuck wheel, with Krishna's questions still in the air and a light rising into the sun. Your line was he hangs his head in shame, and says nothing.

Karna is gone. Bhishma lies on his bed of arrows. Drona is dead. The commanders Duryodhana trusted have fallen one after another, and in the Kaurava camp the king sits among the survivors, grieving. Then an old man speaks up. It's Kripa, the teacher who trained these princes when they were boys, Kaurava and Pandava alike. He doesn't flatter. He tells the king the truth as he sees it.
screen: `KARNA IS GONE.` → `THE COMMANDERS HAVE FALLEN.` → `KRIPA SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Kripa's counsel, in Ganguli's English, is plain: make peace with the Pandavas. Yudhishthira is gentle, he says in effect. He'll let you keep a share of the kingdom. There's still time. And Duryodhana says no. His reasons are worth hearing, because he isn't simply stubborn. He has wronged the Pandavas too deeply, he says, to be trusted now; they would never believe a peace from him. Then something closer to the bone. My friends died for me, the kings and kinsmen who fought at my word. How could I now live in comfort, after sending them to die? He would rather fall the way they fell, as a warrior on the field. It's a terrible answer and, in its way, a loyal one. Then the question: who leads tomorrow? Drona's son Ashvatthama names Shalya, king of Madra, the man who drove Karna's chariot and told him he was the crow. Duryodhana asks him, and Shalya accepts. The driver becomes the commander, and this book of the epic is named for him: the Shalya Parva. The twins' own uncle, who came to the war meaning to fight for their side, will lead the army against them.
screen: `KRIPA SAYS MAKE PEACE` · `TOO LATE TO BE TRUSTED` · `MY FRIENDS DIED FOR ME` · then, large: `SHALYA TAKES COMMAND`

844.title: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
844.hook: the patient brother goes out to fight Shalya, and the dice-master meets Sahadeva
844.carry: the vow from that hall is kept
844.tomorrow: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
844.howItsDone: Yudhishthira's battle with Shalya and Sahadeva's killing of Shakuni are told in the Shalya Parva and in retellings and serials of the Mahabharata, as the moment the war's last vows begin to be kept.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Duryodhana turned down Kripa's plea for peace, and Shalya took command. Your line was it isn't too late.

Who should face Shalya? On the Pandava side, the question goes to Krishna, and his answer is not the obvious one. Not Arjuna. Not Bhima. Yudhishthira: the eldest brother, the one who lost everything at dice, the one Karna sent back to camp humiliated just the day before. Shalya is strong, Krishna says, in effect, and you are the one to meet him. Put away your gentleness for today. And Yudhishthira, the man the epic keeps showing us as patient, picks up his weapons.
screen: `WHO SHOULD FACE SHALYA?` → `NOT ARJUNA. NOT BHIMA.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA.`

segments.voice: The fight is long and fierce, and in Ganguli's English the patient king is almost unrecognizable: steady, fearless, pressing forward. Shalya fights hard too; he has led the army since dawn. At last Yudhishthira takes up a dart, a spear made for throwing, and hurls it with all his strength. It strikes Shalya, and the king of Madra falls to the earth. The man who once held Karna's reins, and then led the whole army himself, lies still on the field. The twins have lost their uncle, at their brother's hand. As Shalya's army breaks, another fight finishes something older. Shakuni, Duryodhana's uncle, the man who threw the dice in the rigged game that cost the Pandavas everything, is still on the field. In the dice hall, years before, the youngest brother Sahadeva had sworn that Shakuni would die by his hand. Now Sahadeva finds him. The dice-master has no dice here. Sahadeva kills him, and the vow from that hall is kept. On a single day, the gentle brother kills a king, and the quiet brother pays back the gambler. The Kaurava army is nearly gone. And Duryodhana, looking around, finds himself almost alone.
screen: `THE PATIENT KING FIGHTS` · `SHALYA FALLS` · `SAHADEVA FINDS SHAKUNI` · then, large: `DURYODHANA ALMOST ALONE`

segments.voice: Sit up, letting your back straighten without strain, and let your face soften while your spine stays tall. Bring to mind something you've been too gentle to face, and meet it in your mind with steadiness, not anger, the kind Yudhishthira found that day. If you pray, you can ask for that steadiness in your own words.
Shalya. The commander who falls to the patient eldest brother, while Sahadeva settles an old vow with the dice-master Shakuni.
Your line: the vow from that hall is kept. The quiet brother remembered. See you tomorrow.

845.title: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
845.hook: the last Kaurava king walks into a lake, and some hunters overhear
845.tomorrow: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
845.howItsDone: Duryodhana's hiding in the lake, told in the Shalya Parva, is retold in readings, regional theater and serials of the Mahabharata, and the lake scene leads into the war's final duel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shalya fell to Yudhishthira's dart, and Sahadeva kept his vow against Shakuni. Your line was the vow from that hall is kept.

One man walks away from the battlefield on foot, carrying a mace. His horse is dead. His army is gone. His brothers, his friends, his commanders have fallen. He is the king the whole war was fought for, and he is alone. On the way he meets Sanjaya, his father's companion, and gives him a message for the blind old king at home: tell my father I've gone into the lake. Then Duryodhana walks down to the water's edge, and keeps walking.
screen: `ALONE, ON FOOT.` → `TELL MY FATHER.` → `INTO THE LAKE.`

segments.voice: In Ganguli's English, Duryodhana enters the lake and, by a power of illusion he knows, binds the waters around him, so that he can rest beneath them, hidden. It's an eerie picture: the lake smooth and still, and the last Kaurava king lying under it. Three survivors of his army find the lake: Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma. They call down to him from the bank. Come out, fight with us. From under the water he answers: not tonight. I'm wounded and tired. Tomorrow. Then the epic brings in some passersby: hunters, men who bring meat to Bhima's kitchen. They hear the whole conversation, a king speaking from under a lake, and they think: the Pandavas are searching everywhere for Duryodhana, and Bhima will reward us. So they go and tell him. The war's last hiding place is given away by a few hunters with a delivery to make. The Pandavas come to the lake with Krishna, and their army fills the shore with noise. Yudhishthira stands at the edge of the still water and speaks to his cousin underneath it. Why are you hiding? Come out and fight. Duryodhana answers from below: I'm not afraid. I'm only resting.
screen: `HE BINDS THE WATERS` · `THREE SURVIVORS CALL DOWN` · `THE HUNTERS OVERHEAR` · then, large: `WHY ARE YOU HIDING?`

846.title: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
846.hook: Duryodhana offers the earth; Yudhishthira refuses it, and makes a risky offer of his own
846.tomorrow: Shalya: Duryodhana in the lake, the mace fight
846.howItsDone: The exchange at the lake, from the Shalya Parva, is retold in readings and serials of the Mahabharata, and Duryodhana's earlier refusal of even a needle's point of land is recalled there.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the Shalya book, Duryodhana lay hidden in the lake until some hunters gave him away. Your line was not afraid, only resting.

An offer rises from under the water. Take the whole earth, Duryodhana says, in effect. My friends are dead, my brothers are dead. I have no wish to rule an empty kingdom. I'll go to the forest, dressed in deerskins, and live there. It sounds like surrender, the end of the war handed over without another blow. And Yudhishthira, standing on the bank, refuses.
screen: `TAKE THE WHOLE EARTH.` → `I'LL GO TO THE FOREST.` → `YUDHISHTHIRA REFUSES.`

segments.voice: It isn't yours to give, Yudhishthira answers, in Ganguli's telling. When we asked for land before the war, you wouldn't give us as much ground as the point of a needle would cover. Now that you've lost it, you offer it all as a gift? A warrior doesn't take a kingdom as charity. Come out and fight. Then he goes further, and it gets dangerous. Choose any one of us, he says, with any weapon you like. Beat that one, and the kingdom is yours. Krishna is alarmed. He tells Yudhishthira he has put everything at risk again, on a single throw, and that none of the brothers but Bhima can match Duryodhana with the mace, and even Bhima has less skill. Some readers hear in this the old dice game coming back: the king who lost everything once by gambling has just gambled again. 847.howItsDone: The mace fight between Bhima and Duryodhana is a favorite scene in retellings, dance-dramas and recitations of the Mahabharata, and Bhima is often shown in art holding his mace.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yudhishthira refused the earth offered from the lake and made a risky offer of his own, and the hidden king came up out of the water to take it. Your line was it isn't yours to give.

Two men face each other on open ground, each holding a heavy iron mace. One is Bhima, of the Pandava brothers. The other is Duryodhana, the Kaurava king, wet from the lake he hid in. Just then a third man arrives, fresh from a long pilgrimage along the holy river Sarasvati. It's Balarama, Krishna's elder brother. He taught both of these men how to fight with the mace. He has stayed out of the whole war. Now he's back in time to watch his two students try to kill each other.
screen: `TWO MEN, TWO MACES.` → `A TEACHER ARRIVES.` → `BOTH ARE HIS STUDENTS.`

segments.voice: Balarama greets everyone, and he asks for the fight to move. In Ganguli's telling, they all walk to Samantapanchaka, ground held holy, so that a warrior who dies there dies in a sacred place. Then the two cousins close in. The epic gives the fight like weather: maces crashing, sparks flying, the two circling each other like bulls. Neither gives way. At the edge of the ground, Arjuna asks Krishna, in effect, which of them is better. Krishna's answer is careful. Bhima is the stronger. Duryodhana has put in more practice and has more skill. Fought by the rules, Bhima may not win. Then Krishna reminds Arjuna of something said years before, in the dice hall. When Draupadi was dragged in and insulted, Duryodhana bared his thigh to her, and Bhima vowed to break that thigh with his mace. Arjuna understands. Standing where Bhima can see him, he strikes his own thigh with his hand. Bhima sees it. When Duryodhana next leaps into the air, Bhima swings low, a blow the rules of mace fighting forbid, and breaks both his thighs. The king falls. This week ran from Karna's stuck wheel, through Shalya's command, to this one blow on a holy plain. And the teacher of both fighters has seen all of it.
